text.p: Silicon Graphics Inc reported operating earnings that were well below Wall Street expectations for its third quarter, adding to a series of consecutive earnings shortfalls, analysts said.

The company reported net earnings per share excluding one-time charges of $0.09 a share, down sharply from $0.31 a share in the year-ago quarter and well below Wall Street's consensus estimate of $0.27 a share, according to First Call.
"Where is the revenue and where are the earnings?" asked one agitated analyst after seeing the earnings report. "This is how many quarters in a row (of disappointments)?"

Silicon Graphics has been struggling for more than a year to regain its financial footing as it also absorbed the acquisition of supercomputing pioneer Cray Research Inc and launched a sweeping upgrade of its entire product line.

The company said revenues for the third quarter of fiscal 1997 to March 31 rose 34 percent to $909 million compared to $677 million a year before, without Cray, or 15 percent on a pro forma basis combined with Cray of $788 million last year.
Shares of Silicon Graphics slipped to a 52-week low of 16-7/8 in trading ahead of the earnings release, closing down 3/8 at 17 on the Nasdaq market.
The earnings release was issued after the close, but traders said Silicon Graphics shares were changing hands in afterhours dealing for as low as 14 -- the lowest level for the stock since 1993.

Silicon Graphics CEO Edward McCracken said in a statement the company had made "good progress" with its transition to the new "O Series" product line and its new high performance Octane desktop workstation had shipped in limited volume.
But analysts said they expected a conference call with company executives this afternoon to be somber after the string of shortfalls at SGI dating back to late 1995.
"Nobody really has any faith in this company," one analyst said. "Nobody has any expectations."

McCracken offered little further explanation of the reasons behind the shortfall in a tersely worded statement issued by the company, but he cited "healthy server demand from industrial, commercial and governmental customers."

Silicon Graphics has been a pioneer in the area of computing-intensive graphics workstations, but is expected to face increasing pressure from other, cheaper computer systems, including high-end personal computers running on Intel Corp's microprocessors.
